title: Family heritage album layout
subtitle: Designing a page layout for old family photographs and handwritten documents
excerpt: Family heritage scrapbooking preserves photographs and documents that are often fragile, in poor condition, or irreplaceable. The layout decisions must work around what already exists: odd photo sizes, mismatched documents, and handwriting that needs to stay readable. Restraint is the design principle: the heritage material is the content; the layout supports it without competing.
sourceNotes: Family heritage scrapbooking technique is a contemporary archival and craft practice. This entry is an original Homemade design drawing on archival mounting standards.

glossaryTerms.definition: A small paper or mylar triangular pocket adhered to a scrapbook page to hold photograph corners without touching the photograph surface with adhesive. The photograph can be removed from the corners at any time without damage.

A narrow strip of acid-free paper placed below a photograph or document with handwritten identification text. The strip is attached to the page, not to the photograph, so the photograph remains undamaged.

content.text: Start with one rule: never glue original photographs or documents directly to any page.

items.name: Scrapbook album with acid-free pages
items.notes: An album with removable pages (ring binder or post-bound) is better for heritage use than a sewn album: pages can be added, reorganised, or duplicated for family sharing.

items.name: Archival photo corners, clear mylar or acid-free paper
items.notes: Clear mylar corners are less visible; acid-free paper corners can be colour-matched to the page. Both must be labelled as archival quality.

items.name: Acid-free card stock for captioning strips
items.notes: Cut 20 to 30 mm wide strips from any acid-free card. These are the captioning strips.

items.name: Fine-liner, 0.38 mm, archival quality
items.notes: For writing captions. Archival ink only: ordinary ballpoint or felt-tip inks are not stable over decades.

items.name: Acid-free PVA adhesive
items.notes: For mounting captioning strips and photo corners to the page only, never to photographs.

content.text: Place only one to three photographs per page. Heritage photographs often have different aspect ratios, and crowding them together makes the page look disordered. Allow generous white space around each photograph. A single large photograph with a captioning strip below it and a short handwritten annotation on the opposite page is more effective than six small photographs competing for space on one page.

Write the photograph identification on the captioning strip in standard format: names, date, location, occasion. Use the full name for everyone pictured, not initials or nicknames that may not be understood by future generations. If the date is uncertain, write 'approximately [decade]' rather than leaving the date blank. Glue the captioning strip to the page immediately below the photograph corners. Do not write on the back of original photographs: any writing medium will migrate through the photograph paper over time.

items.symptom: The old photographs are faded or damaged — should they be placed in the album as they are?
items.fix: Scan all originals at high resolution before placing anything in the album. If originals are very fragile, put only the scans in the album. Store the originals flat in acid-free envelopes in a dark, cool, dry place. The scans are for use; the originals are the archive.
